content: Acid indigestion, also known as dyspepsia, is a condition characterized by an excessive amount of hydrochloric acid in the stomach. If it occurs frequently, it can irritate the stomach lining or the duodenum, potentially leading to ulcers, which may become life-threatening. However, it is important to note that the majority of stomach ulcers (approximately 85-95%) are caused by infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori rather than by excessive stomach acid. Acid indigestion is distinct from heartburn, which typically involves irritation of the esophagus. Causes of Acid Indigestion Common causes of acid indigestion include consuming foods high in fat or spice, excessive alcohol or caffeine intake, smoking, overeating, and eating late at night or just before sleeping. Over-the-counter antacids are widely available for symptom relief, but overuse can lead to dependency and other complications. Certain medications and substances are also associated with acid indigestion, including: Drugs like adefovir, duloxetine, lithium, and simvastatin. Substances such as garlic, niacin, and vitamin C. Conditions like hookworm infection, Gulf War syndrome, and primary hyperparathyroidism. Historical Perspective Acid indigestion was first described in the 1980s as discomfort in the upper abdomen (epigastric region) or behind the sternum (retrosternal area) lasting more than four weeks. Patients were categorized into subtypes based on symptoms and underlying mechanisms: reflux-like, ulcer-like, dysmotility-like, and unspecified dyspepsia. Reflux-like dyspepsia was later reclassified as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) unless proven otherwise. Acid indigestion is now defined as epigastric pain without a specific duration. Classification According to the Rome II classification, acid indigestion is divided into three subtypes: 1. Ulcer-like dyspepsia: Characterized by significant pain in the upper abdomen. 2. Dysmotility-like dyspepsia: Non-painful discomfort such as bloating, nausea, or early satiety. 3. Unspecified dyspepsia: Symptoms that do not fit into the other categories. Pathophysiology The exact mechanisms underlying acid indigestion remain unclear, but several factors are thought to contribute: Gastrointestinal motor abnormalities: These include delayed gastric emptying, uneven food distribution in the stomach, and impaired stomach motility, which can lead to nausea, vomiting, or gastric distension. Altered visceral sensation: Patients may experience heightened sensitivity to normal physiological stimuli, both during fasting and after meals. This may involve impaired relaxation of the stomach or increased sensitivity of the stomach lining. Psychosocial factors: Anxiety and changes in circadian rhythm have been linked to acid indigestion. Patients with high anxiety levels are at greater risk, and somatic complaints may also play a role. Infections: Post-infectious conditions, such as bacterial, viral, or parasitic gastroenteritis, can lead to symptoms of acid indigestion. Helicobacter pylori: This bacterium is strongly associated with acid indigestion and ulcers. Genetics: A family history of abdominal pain may suggest a genetic predisposition, though this has not been definitively proven. Differentiating Acid Indigestion from Other Conditions Acid indigestion must be distinguished from other conditions with similar symptoms, such as: Gastroduodenal ulcers Reflux esophagitis Atypical GERD Biliary tract disease Pancreatitis Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) Medication-induced dyspepsia Gastric cancer A thorough medical history and physical examination are essential for differentiation, and diagnostic tools like endoscopy may be required. Epidemiology and Demographics Acid indigestion is a common condition affecting individuals of all ages, though most studies focus on adults over 18. Prevalence peaks between the ages of 45-54 in Western populations, while in Chinese and Japanese populations, it peaks slightly later. Subtypes of acid indigestion may vary by age group, with ulcer-like dyspepsia more common in younger individuals and dysmotility-like dyspepsia in older adults. The condition affects men and women equally, though some studies suggest a higher prevalence in women. Risk Factors Key risk factors for acid indigestion include: Excessive alcohol consumption Smoking Overuse of medications like aspirin and antidepressants Peptic ulcer disease Psychosocial factors such as anxiety and somatization Diagnosis The diagnosis of acid indigestion is made after ruling out other conditions. Diagnostic methods include: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD): To identify abnormalities in the esophagus, stomach, or small intestine. Nutrient Meal Test: A non-invasive test to assess symptoms like epigastric pain, bloating, and nausea. Differentiation from gastroparesis and GERD: Imaging studies and endoscopy can help distinguish these conditions. Brain imaging: Techniques like PET and fMRI are being explored to assess potential brain-gut interactions. Symptoms Common symptoms of acid indigestion include: Epigastric pain Nausea and vomiting Upper abdominal fullness or bloating Anxiety and distress Less common symptoms include an acidic taste in the mouth, belching, and a burning sensation in the upper abdomen. Physical Examination and Laboratory Findings Physical examination findings are often normal, though epigastric tenderness may be present. Additional assessments may include: Hemodynamic evaluation to rule out blood loss. Stool analysis for abnormalities. Examination of the oral cavity for signs of GERD or dental erosion. Abdominal examination for signs of biliary tract disease or malignancy. Laboratory tests may include a complete blood count (CBC), liver function tests, and tests for H. pylori infection. Treatment Treatment focuses on symptom relief and improving overall health. Key approaches include: Dietary modifications: Avoiding trigger foods, reducing fat intake, and eating slowly. Pharmacological therapy: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are the first-line treatment, followed by H2 receptor antagonists and, in some cases, antidepressants like tricyclics or mirtazapine. H. pylori eradication: If H. pylori is identified, targeted antibiotic therapy is the definitive treatment. Psychological support: Placebo treatments have shown benefits in some cases, particularly when psychological factors are involved. Surgery is rarely indicated for acid indigestion. Avoiding foods and beverages that trigger symptoms. Reducing alcohol and caffeine consumption. Quitting smoking. Practicing good sleep hygiene.
